span.span: Controller Design Methodology from Training-Set Traces

1. Evidence and scope:
Read the strategy guide before inspecting traces. Use aggregate summaries first, then inspect bounded representative cases and anomalous groups. The evidence consists of executed training-set policies; raw questions, gold answers, private caches, and unexecuted checkpoints remain outside the evidence.

2. Calibrate the replay cost model:
Estimate the mean phase latency from the trace summary and estimate tokens per continue action from aggregate action counts. Use the authoritative model weights and the current env.requirements. Parallel spawn_many and continue_many use cohort maxima for latency, whereas weighted compute is summed over all branches. These estimates are heuristic because the scorer uses maximum per-question latency within each seed batch and accounts for action-level variation.

3. Optimize the joint hard-constraint utility:
A seed batch is satisfied only when accuracy, latency, and weighted compute all pass simultaneously. The optimization target is the profile-weighted fraction of satisfied batches, and proposal acceptance is strict improvement over the incumbent. Per-constraint satisfaction rates and margins diagnose failures; joint satisfaction rate (JSR) remains the acceptance criterion.

4. Construct a feasible policy before optimizing quality:
Try several (width, loop_limit) combinations at the current model using the calibrated estimates. If none is feasible, move to a lighter model. The default controller structure is parallel initial spawning, parallel continuation rounds, and deterministic plurality voting over usable final answers. A zero continuation limit is valid when the budget permits only spawn actions.

5. Match depth and width to the bottleneck:
In the observed math-reasoning traces, accuracy is the most common bottleneck. Increase depth when branches remain active at the loop limit and accuracy is binding; reduce depth when resources bind and branches terminate earlier. Width primarily adds voting diversity and should increase only when compute headroom supports it.

6. Treat early stopping and refine as conditional mechanisms:
Use confidence-based early stopping or refinement only when the relevant budget and failure diagnosis justify it. Early stopping trades latency for accuracy, while refinement adds tokens and latency; verify the joint utility after either change.

7. Diagnose failures before changing parameters:
After a failed round, read per-constraint satisfaction rates and margins, then check whether the loop limit was actually reached. Small negative margins call for an incremental change of one or two rounds or branches; large gaps call for recalibration from the new trace summary. Do not assume that fixing the lowest individual satisfaction rate will improve the joint rate, because different seed batches can fail on different constraints.

8. Reallocate only verified headroom:
Latency headroom can support a small increase in continuation depth, and compute headroom can support a small increase in branch width, but both changes must be checked against the other constraints. Reducing depth or width to exploit accuracy headroom is risky because terminal-answer quality can change non-linearly.

9. Generalization and limits:
The guide summarizes 488 failed proposals, 800 observed transitions, and 200 training profiles. These statistics define its empirical scope; preserve determinism, use public observations, and re-estimate costs and joint satisfaction after each meaningful policy change.
